summary: Grindle Point Light on Islesboro: an 1850 brick light rebuilt in 1875, given a steel tower in 1934, relit in 1987, and open again since its 2025 reopening.

access.note: The Town of Islesboro owns the station. The tower is open in summer, and the museum has summer hours.

events.note: Congress appropriated $3,500 on 3 March 1849 for a lighthouse at Islesboro
Brick tower (28 ft) and keeper's house completed in the summer of 1850
USLHS gives 1850 as the year established
Fifth-order Fresnel lens placed in the lantern (LighthouseFriends)
Tower and keeper's dwelling rebuilt; the old house became a covered way (NRHP 1875 report); USLHS gives the tower year as 1874
New boathouse (LighthouseFriends)
Brick cistern built into the covered passage
Barn rebuilt; premises enclosed by a wire fence after the deed dispute
Boundary error in the 1849 deed resolved; $79.30 in legal fees
1,000-pound fog bell struck by hand, recorded 3 October 1896 (LighthouseFriends gives 1897)
New oil house (LighthouseFriends)
Keeper James E. Hall died at the station after a blasting accident (LighthouseFriends)
Decommissioned 30 June 1933 (LighthouseFriends); the NRHP and USLHS date the automation to 1934
21-foot steel tower built to carry a flashing white light (NRHP)
Acquired by the Town of Islesboro for a park and museum (NRHP); LighthouseFriends gives a $1,200 sale in 1934
Sailors' Memorial Museum established in the keeper's quarters (LighthouseFriends)
Entered in the National Register on 13 March 1987
Relighting ceremony 4 November 1987 with a solar-powered optic; skeleton tower torn down (LighthouseFriends)
LED VLB-44 optic installed in January 2017
Tower repairs cost $228,000 (LighthouseFriends)
Tower reopened to the public 29 June 2025 after six years closed

corrections.why: The station was relit in 1987 with a solar optic and given an LED optic in 2017 (LighthouseFriends; USLHS 'Current Optic ... installed 2017'). The NRHP (1987) describes the automated light as functioning as a navigational aid.
The NRHP describes a flashing white light in 1934, and LighthouseFriends a flashing green light since 1987. Check the current Light List before changing the record.

corrections.proposed: tower, square brick, built 1875, 11.9 m (39 ft), standing; the 1850 brick tower was 28 ft and was replaced
corrections.why: The 1850 tower was 28 ft (NRHP). The brick tower of 1874-75 is 39 ft (LighthouseFriends; USLHS 39 ft).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1850 tower was rebuilt in 1874-75 (NRHP 1875 report; USLHS tower year 1874). The record's 1850 is the first light; the 1874-75 tower is the one standing.
LighthouseFriends gives decommissioning on 30 June 1933; the NRHP and USLHS give 1934 for the automation and steel tower. The record's 1934 follows the NRHP.

The NRHP appointed Rufus Dunning on 20 August 1850; Farrow (quoted by LighthouseFriends) names him first; the archive agrees. Francis Grindle's start is 1852 in the archive and 3 April 1853 in the NRHP.

notes_for_editor: Keepers come from the USLHS roster (NARA registers via the Kraig Anderson inventory). The match was by name and by a position about 982 km away from the station, so it is unreliable on position; the archive's Grindle Point place record has a wrong longitude (-56.6). The keeper rows are not yet confirmed in primary records. Keeper dates disagree: the NRHP puts Dunning's appointment at 20 August 1850 and Grindle's replacement of him at 3 April 1853; the archive has Grindell 1852. The archive lists V. I. Trundy in 1908 only; no source read says who she was. The 1916 accident rests on LighthouseFriends alone. Chronicling America searches for 1916 returned HTTP 520 errors from loc.gov for the matching pages, so it was not confirmed in a newspaper; the story attributes it to LighthouseFriends. Dates disagree about the end of the lighthouse: LighthouseFriends says it was decommissioned on 30 June 1933 and sold for $1,200 in 1934 and that the museum opened in 1938; the NRHP says the steel tower was built in 1934 and the town acquired the site in 1935; the USLHS says discontinued 1934 to 1987. The 1896 bell is dated 3 October 1896 in the 1897 Light-House Board report (scan 265); LighthouseFriends gives 1897. The record's status 'inactive' conflicts with the light being relit in 1987 and given an LED optic in 2017 (USLHS, LighthouseFriends). The record's characteristic (F W) and range (4 nm) are not in any source read here; the NRHP gives a flashing white light for the 1934 steel tower and LighthouseFriends a flashing green light since 1987. The Town of Islesboro museum page gives summer hours that differ from LighthouseFriends' Friday to Sunday. The story gives both sets of hours and does not choose between them. James E. Hall: LighthouseFriends says he came from Matinicus Rock, but gives no years, so no other_stations entry is made. The record's tower height (12.0 m) matches the 1874-75 tower (39 ft, LighthouseFriends and USLHS), not the 1850 tower (28 ft, NRHP). Verification 2026-10-22: the Board's FY1891 deed entry (scan p.50) is OCR'd with garbled words; the quoted words are its readable part. The FY1892 legal-services line (scan p.346: $79.30 for correcting error in title to Grindel Point) and the premises line (scan p.376) read cleanly. The FY1897 bell lines (scan p.265, 3 October 1896; scan p.293, bell established) match. The NRHP quotes the 1875 Board annual report; the story attributes that to the nomination, not to the Board directly. The archive's 1906 oil house date and LighthouseFriends' 1905 are both stated in the story. Page images were not viewed; the FY1891 deed entry (scan p.50) and the FY1897 bell lines (scans 265, 293) were read from cached OCR. The roster is matched by name only (roster.py warning: USLHS position 982 km away), so the keeper rows depend on the name match and should be checked against the archive's own page.
